item30: The original study did not report descriptive statistics needed for accurate power analysis. Based on the original study’s findings, β = -.19, b = -.32, SE b = .16, p = .043, we conducted a power analysis to confirm our required sample size.  Our replication of the original study’s simple linear regression in study 2 found that β = 0.003,  b = 0.004. SE b = 0.139, p = 0.976. The resultant regression equation was found to be insignificant and the estimations for the coefficients will thereby be inaccurate representations of the true effect. Pearson’s correlation was also low (r = .003, p = .976) and as such, we can conclude that was no significant linear relationship between maximising tendency and inaction inertia. Similar results were observed for the logistic regression, e^β = 1.05, p = .825. The lack of significance suggested that the effects were negligible when using maximising tendency to predict inaction inertia on the dichotomous item. Thus, since the measures for effect size in our regression (namely the Pearson’s correlation values and the coefficients) were insignificant, there was no linear relationship between maximising tendency and inaction inertia.

item31: Findings of regressing inaction inertia on maximising tendency did not reject the null hypothesis, R2=.000, F(1, 119) = .001, p > .05,  95% CI [-.270, .279]. 80% CI [-.175, .183].

item32: not significantly different from the original effect size

item33: informative failure to replicate

item34: Since we have defined a successful replication to be an exact or the closest possible replication of the original study, our replication could be judged to be a partial success. 
On one hand, by carrying out the replication study as close to the original as possible, the participants in our sample experienced the same intended stimulus as the participants in the US population of the original study. Recruited participants were all measured using the same scale (MTS) and judged on the same criteria as the original study. Besides, the instructions and procedure participants went through were similar to the original study. Ultimately, we created the closest replication possible such that the only differences were those that were impractical for researchers to control. Hence, the process of replicating the study was a success in following the original as closely as possible. 
On the other hand, our replication study faced informative limitations such as inadequate information given by the original authors, as well as practical limitations which can be attributed to the lack of resources such as providing remuneration. These limitations might have affected results and thus, we cannot judge our replication study to be a complete success. 

The failure of replication can be attributed partly to inadequate amount of information.   Lack of relevant details in the original paper, such as descriptive statistics, makes it difficult for present researchers to accurately estimate the required number of participants needed for a replication study with adequate power to sufficiently replicate the original effect. 

Furthermore, the time given to complete the replication study (10 weeks) was insufficient to gather a large enough sample size for the recommended power statistic of 1-β = .8. In addition, there were limitations in resources, unlike the original study whereby participants were paid. We were unable to provide monetary remuneration or any form of incentives to our participants for the completion of the survey materials. Hence, the lack of resources to incentivise might have caused the difference in results from the original study. This may be attributed to attentional differences since 128 responses were removed as a result of failing at least one manipulative or quality check, as compared to eight responses being excluded in the original study.

We judge this replication as inconclusive since the replication study will not find any statistically significantly results due to the limitations present. Hence, it might not be possible to conclude if maximizing tendency was related to inaction inertia in a job offer context, based on our study alone.

item37: One limitation was our sample population. We conducted the replication study in Singapore, whereby undergraduates were conveniently sampled on a university campus. This differed from the original study, where it was conducted in the United States using a participant pool from Amazon’s MTurk, a survey platform. Hence, our sample population was younger (M = 24.21, compared to M = 27.97 of the original sample), and they have fewer work experiences. As such, these undergraduates might possibly have a lower likelihood of experiencing inaction inertia as they seek work experiences and view the increase in salary as more attractive. Thus, the differences in sample populations might have caused bias in the measure of inaction inertia, hence influencing results. Besides, another limitation of our replication could be due to a small sample size of 121 participants, which reduced the possibility of detecting a significant effect because of a low statistical power. Furthermore, given that our sample participants were not incentivised to complete the survey, the lack of quality responses could have resulted in the differences in results observed. This was evidenced by the large quantity of participants that we had to exclude in our analysis compared to the original study. It was also possible that the recruited participants might not have a full understanding of the stimulus materials, which contributed to the lack of quality responses.

title_r: High Quality Direct Replications Matter: Response to Williams (2014)
abstract_r: We respond to Williams’ (2014) comments on our three failures to replicate of Study 2 fromWilliams and Bargh (2008). We clarify our conclusions on this topic, making clear that although the results of our studies cast doubt on the specific effect reported in Williams and Bargh (i.e., that instant hot and cold packs influence choice of reward for self or friend), a more complete understanding of the embodiment hypothesis in question requires consideration of relevant conceptual replications. Accordingly, we consider the strength of the evidence in the conceptual replications that Williams identifies and find that small samples appear to be the norm. We conclude that in order for researchers to move forward, future studies must take seriously issues of power, researcher degrees of freedom, and file drawer problems. Doing so will ensure that future studies are more informative tests of this hypothesis.

title_r: Is There a Positive Association between Working Memory Capacity and Mind Wandering in a Low-Demand Breathing Task? A Preregistered Replication of Levinson, Smallwood, and Davidson (2012)
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

Levinson, Smallwood, and Davidson (2012, Experiment 2) found that working memory capacity (WMC) correlated positively with mind-wandering propensity measured by thought probes in a breath-monitoring task, but was unassociated with the tendency to self-catch mind-wandering. Here, I sought to replicate the associations between mind-wandering and WMC in the Levinson et al. breath task. With data from a large sample of subjects and two measures of WMC, the data from the current study suggests that, if WMC correlates with probe-caught mind wandering, it is most likely negative. In addition, the evidence regarding self-caught mind wandering is consistent with Levinson et al. for the sum of self-caught responses, but when self-caught responses are considered in proportion to probe-caught mind wandering, modest evidence was found for a positive association with WMC.

title_r: No Evidence for Unethical Amnesia for Imagined Actions: A Failed Replication and Extension
abstract_r: In a recent paper, Kouchaki and Gino (2016) suggest that memory for unethical actions is impaired, regardless of whether such actions are real or imagined. However, as we argue in the current paper, their claim that people develop “unethical amnesia” confuses two distinct and dissociable memory deficits: one affecting the phenomenology of remembering and another affecting memory accuracy. To further investigate whether unethical amnesia affects memory accuracy, we conducted three studies exploring unethical amnesia for imagined ethical violations. The first study (N = 228) attempts to directly replicate the only study from Kouchaki and Gino (2016) that includes a measure of memory accuracy. The second study (N = 232) attempts again to replicate these accuracy effects from Kouchaki and Gino (2016), while including several additional variables meant to potentially help in finding the effect. The third study (N = 228) is an attempted conceptual replication using the same paradigm as Kouchaki and Gino (2016), but with a new vignette describing a different moral violation. We did not find an unethical amnesia effect involving memory accuracy in any of our three studies. These results cast doubt upon the claim that memory accuracy is impaired for imagined unethical actions. Suggestions for further ways to study memory for moral and immoral actions are discussed.

title_r: Intuitive judgments in depression and the role of processing fluency and positive valence: A preregistered replication study
abstract_r: Background: Recent preliminary evidence indicates that depression is associated with impaired intuitive information processing. The current study aimed at replicating these findings and to move one step further by exploring whether factors known as triggering intuition (positivity, processing fluency) also affect intuition in patients with depression. Method: We pre-registered and tested five hypotheses using data from 35 patients with depression and 35 healthy controls who performed three versions of the Judgment of Semantic Coherence Task (JSCT, Bowers et al., 1990). This task operationalizes intuition as the inexplicable and sudden detection of semantic coherence. Results: Results revealed that depressed patients and healthy controls did not differ in their general intuitive performance (Hypothesis 1). We further found that fluency did not significantly affect depressed patients’ coherence judgments (H2a) and that the assumed effect of fluency on coherence judgments was not moderated by depression (H2b). Finally, we found that triads positive in valence were more likely to be judged as coherent as compared to negative word triads in the depressed sample (H3a), but this influence of positive (vs. negative) valence on coherence judgments did not significantly differ between the two groups (H3b). Conclusion: Overall the current study did not replicate findings from previous research regarding intuitive semantic coherence detection deficits in depression. However, our findings suggest that enhancing positivity in depressed patients may facilitate their ability to see meaning in their environment and to take intuitive decision.

title_r: Testing the Replicability of the Theory of Planned Behavior: A Large-Scale Multi-Sample Registered Replication Study
abstract_r: Identifying the determinants of social behavior, and the specific processes by which the determinants relate to behavior, are important in the development of theory to predict social behavior. Predicting behavior also has utility for organizations and stakeholders interested in developing effective interventions and strategies to promote behavior change. The theory of planned behavior (Ajzen, 1991) is a prominent social psychological theory developed to predict social behavior. The theory derives its assumptions from theories of attitude and social cognition (Albarracín & Johnson, 2019; Eagly & Chaiken, 1993; Fishbein, 1967), and focuses on predicting intentional behavior from sets of beliefs about future behavioral engagement. The theory has been tested in over 2000 studies, and over 30 meta-analytic syntheses. Cumulative findings indicate its efficacy in accounting for variance in behaviors across multiple domains. However, considerable unresolved heterogeneity in effects has been observed, which could be attributable to methodological artifacts or genuine variability across contexts, behaviors, and populations. In addition, some theory predictions, particularly interactions among constructs, have not been tested and replicated consistently. The current project will conduct a large-scale replication of the theory in general population and student samples adopting an identical protocol and measures. The result of the study will be a series of data sets testing theory predictions analyzed by meta-analytic structural equation modeling.

title_r: Acquiring the cardinal knowledge of number words: A conceptual replication
abstract_r: Understanding the way in which counting represent numerosities was shown to be a long-lasting process. As shown in the Give-a-number task, acquiring the meanings of verbal number words goes through successive developmental stages in which children first learn the cardinal meanings of small number words one at a time before generalizing the cardinal principle they have induced from the first three number words to all number words within their counting range. This acquisition would take about a year, and would be completed by the age of 3 ½ years. The aim of the present study was to provide a conceptual replication of the developmental sequence described in Wynn’s study nearly 30 years ago using the Give-a-number task. A first cross-sectional study was conducted on 213 Belgian children aged between 39 and 74 months using the Give-a-number task to examine the developmental pattern and the influence of age on this acquisition. The time span of acquisition was examined in a second study in which 34 children were tested five times every months between the age of 36 to 52 months. Results showed that acquiring the cardinal meanings of number words spread out over a protracted period, far more extended than assumed by Wynn. Furthermore, children do not generalize all-at-once to large number words, the cardinal knowledge they learned on small number words. Rather, number words were found to be learned one at a time in a really progressive manner. Results were discussed with regard to their implications for the existing theories and in relation with other tasks assessing the acquisition of verbal number symbols.

title_r: Re‑examining the effect of wage delegation : a replication study of Charness et al. (2012)
abstract_r: Experimental research has explored the effects of wage delegation on employee performance, with the pioneering attempt by (Charness et al., Am Econ Rev 102:2358–2379, 2012) in “The Hidden Advantage of Delegation: Pareto Improvements in a Gift Exchange Game”, published in the American Economic Review. We conducted a replication of their experiment for two main reasons: first, to validate the original findings that have influenced subsequent research, and second, to examine whether these results hold in contexts with reduced social proximity between workers and employers, a relevant issue due to the rise of remote work. Our online experiment, involving 410 participants, followed the original study’s design but used a different sample. We successfully replicated the main finding that wage delegation increases employee effort, though the effect was smaller and largely due to employees granting themselves higher wages. These results support the notion that with decreasing social proximity, formal controls increase in importance.

title_r: Model vs System Level Testing of Autonomous Driving Systems: A Replication and Extension Study
abstract_r: Offline model-level testing of autonomous driving software is much cheaper, faster, and diversified than in-field, online system-level testing. Hence, researchers have compared empirically model-level vs system-level testing using driving simulators. They reported the general usefulness of simulators at reproducing the same conditions experienced in-field, but also some inadequacy of model-level testing at exposing failures that are observable only in online mode. In this work, we replicate the reference study on model vs system-level testing of autonomous vehicles while acknowledging several assumptions that we had reconsidered. These assumptions are related to several threats to validity affecting the original study that motivated additional analysis and the development of techniques to mitigate them. Moreover, we also extend the replicated study by evaluating the original findings when considering a physical, radio-controlled autonomous vehicle. Our results show that simulator-based testing of autonomous driving systems yields predictions that are close to the ones of real-world datasets when using neural-based translation to mitigate the reality gap induced by the simulation platform. On the other hand, model-level testing failures are in line with those experienced at the system level, both in simulated and physical environments, when considering the pre-failure site, similar-looking images, and accurate labels.

title_r: Do Stereotypes Simplify Cognitive Processing? Examining The Cognitive Toolbox Through A Replication And Extension Of Macrae et al. (1994)
abstract_r: Stereotyping occurs in a wide variety of situations and can have severe and negative consequences. One potential explanation for the function of stereotypes offered by Macrae et al. (1994) is that they allow easier mental categorization of individuals and alleviate cognitive load. This can result in more attention for other tasks. In this thesis, I replicated Macrae et al.’s (1994) Study 1 using similar materials and procedures, while also addressing potential limitations to their research. Macrae et al. (1994) found that providing stereotype labels facilitated performance on a secondary task. In my replication study, I found no such facilitation effects. Further research needs to be done to fully understand the relationship between stereotyping and its potential to relieve cognitive load, but my study casts doubt on the reliability of Macrae et al.’s (1994) findings.

title_r: Giving and taking in dictator games – differences by gender? A replication study of Chowdhury et al. (Southern Economic Journal, 2017)
abstract_r: These data and code reproduce the results presented in the paper "Giving and taking in dictator games – differences by gender? A replication study of Chowdhury et al. Abstract: This study attempts to replicate experimental results from Chowdhury et al. published in Southern Economic Journal (2017). They study gender differences in the giving and taking variants of the dictator game. Using the same experimental design on a sample of German students our findings differ from Chowdhury et al. (2017). In contrast to the original study, we do not find support for an asymmetric gender effect. Our results indicate that, on average, both men and women allocate similar amounts in the giving and in the taking frame. title_r: Historical Communist Party Strength and Modern Party Loyalty. A Replication Study of Barceló (PNAS, 2021)
abstract_r: Replication data for “The Long-term Effects of War Exposure on Civic Engagement,” published September 2021, and “Corrections for Barceló, The Long-term Effects of War Exposure on Civic Engagement,” published online July 2023 and February 2024, in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The corrections purport to address several issues in a 2021 publication, which we raised with both PNAS and the author. As we describe in our replication study, the corrections are themselves flawed and continue to lead to misleading findings. Barceló commits three major errors that render his research design inappropriate and his conclusions problematic. First, Barceló again commits a critical coding error that again leads him to attest incorrectly that he is clustering standard errors (SEs) at the provincial level, when in fact he is only using robust SEs, leading to false assertions of statistical significance and instrument strength. Second, Barceló miscodes his measure of South Vietnam. Third, Barceló overfits his model by including a linear transformation of his instrumental variable as a control. When these mistakes are addressed the provocative findings no longer hold.

title_r: A Conceptual replication of the differential price framing effect in the field
abstract_r: Across a series of 10 laboratory and online studies, Allard, Hardisty, and Griffin (2019) demonstrated an increased preference for premium, higher-priced products over standard products when consumers were presented with the additional cost of the higher-priced option (i.e., differential price framing; e.g., “for $20 more”) rather than with its total price (i.e., inclusive price framing; e.g., “for $60 total”); a phenomenon referred to as the differential price framing effect. In this paper, we conceptually replicate this effect in a field experiment that focuses on the application of a differential price framing strategy to a specific product format; namely, multipacks of identical products. Consistent with the differential price framing effect, the present study shows—based on 45,626 add-to-cart events and 30,426 completed product purchases on an online retailer’s website—that the choice shares of higher-priced options increase when a differential price framing strategy is used. However, compared to non-consequential add-to-cart activities, this bias is considerably less pronounced in actual purchase patterns.

title_r: Disgust and the rubber hand illusion: A registered replication report of Jalal, Krishnakumar, and Ramachandran (2015)
abstract_r: Heightened experience of disgust is a feature of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), particularly in contamination-related OCD (C-OCD). Previous studies of the rubber hand illusion (RHI) reported that the sense of body ownership is related to the interaction between vision, touch, and proprioception. A recent study demonstrated a link between the RHI and disgust, reporting an interaction between these three perceptual modalities and disgust (Jalal, Krishnakumar, Ramachandran, 2015). However, there have been no direct replications of this initial study. We proposed a direct replication of Jalal et al.’s (2015) study. Based on a power analysis, we examined a minimum of 119 participants to determine whether placing contamination-related stimuli on a rubber hand causes OCD-like disgust among healthy participants while experiencing the RHI. In addition, we tested the cross-cultural validity of the previous findings, testing whether Japanese participants experience more intense disgust when a rubber hand and a participant’s hidden hand were stroked synchronously, compared with asynchronous stroking. This replication provides insight into potential applications of this study protocol in the treatment of OCD.

summary: SEE WORD DOCUMENT FILE FOR FORMATTED SUBMISSION THAT INCLUDES TABLES/FIGURES

Study Title: Do Expectations and Perceptions of Personality Trait Change in College Students Match Reality?  

Authors: Andrew Rakhshani, Brent Donnellan, Richard Lucas, Courtney Brecheen, & Robert Ackerman

Description: 
	This study aims to conceptually replicate two studies (Herbst, McCrae, Costa, Feaganes, & Siegler, 2000; Robins, Noftle, Trzesniewski, & Roberts, 2005) that compared perceived versus actual personality change and extend these works by also evaluating anticipatory personality change. We will conduct secondary analyses on a large, longitudinal dataset of a student cohort followed across four years of college. We intend to emulate the analyses described in each of the target studies and conduct additional analyses relating to anticipated personality change.
	Herbst and colleagues (2000) sought to determine whether self-reported perceived change in personality was associated with actual changes based on 6 to 9-year follow-up data of middle-aged adults. Participants completed the 240-item NEO-PI-R at baseline and again at follow-up. At follow-up participants were also asked to report on how they had changed since their intake using two measures of change. The first was a single item measure reflecting three perceived change groups (i.e., changed a good deal, changed little, or stayed pretty much the same). The second asked whether participants increased, decreased, or stayed the same on each of the Big 5 dimensions (e.g., Extraversion: “compared to how you were six years ago, how lively, cheerful, and sociable are you now?”). Analyses and results were presented as follows: 
(1) frequencies of perceived change groups (52% stayed the same, 39% changed a little, 9% changed a good deal); 
(2) chi-square test of perceived change groups by gender (men: 54% stayed the same, 38% changed a little, 8% changed a good deal; women: 48% stayed the same, 41% changed a little, 11% changed a good deal; slightly more women reported change 2(2, N = 2,241) = 7.7, p = .02);
(3) compared stability coefficients across perceived change groups by Big 5 factor (see table below); 
 
(4) compared profile stability coefficients across perceived change groups (see table above); 
(5) compared baseline and post (respectively) factor and facet (cannot replicate) scores across perceived change groups (specific effect sizes were not reported; Respondents who felt they had changed a good deal scored significantly higher in Neuroticism and Openness and lower on Agreeableness than the other two groups on both administrations); 
(6) frequencies of perceived factor-level change (see note in table below); 
 
(7) compared mean level change from baseline to follow-up by direction of perceived change (the factor level perceived change measure) using repeated measures ANOVAs with Scheffe post hoc tests (these effect sizes were reported as partial eta squared for Time by perceived change group interaction; see table above); 
(8) correlation of perceived change by domain and residual gain score (“the raw change score corrected for initial level”) for the same domain (All five correlations were positive and significant, ranging in magnitude of .10 for Agreeableness to .24 for Neuroticism; On average, perceptions of change accounted for less than 3% of the variance in measured change); and 
(9) percentage of discordance of perceived change group and actual change (Same group had significant declines in all but Agreeableness; More group increased only in Neuroticism and Agreeableness; Less group showed significant declines in all but A; 80% of the comparisons are discordant for the self-perceived Same group, 60% for the More group, 20% for the Less group).
	
Robins and colleagues (2005) sought to determine (1) the extent and in what ways young adults think their personality changes and (2) how much perceived change was associated with actual change. Their study included a third purpose involving a host of additional measures that our dataset does not include so everything to follow will reflect the two parts we can replicate. They followed a group of 295 young adults for six waves across four years of college. Participants completed the 60-item NEO-FFI during the first week of college and again at the end of the fourth year. At the end of the fourth year, participants were also asked to indicate how they had changed (1 = decreased to 5 = increased) since entering college using a single item for each Big 5 factor. To assess actual personality change, they regressed each year four factor score on the corresponding week one factor score and saved the standardized residuals. Relevant analyses were presented as follows: 
(10) frequencies of perceived change grouped by decreased, stayed the same, and increased for each Big 5 factor (Almost everyone (98%) believed that they had changed on at least one factor; see table below); 
(11) actual mean-level personality change reported as Cohen’s d (see table below); 

 
(12) correlations between perceived and actual change by Big 5 factor (see table below); and 
 
(13) footnote noting comparisons of the intercorrelations among perceived changes and the intercorrelations among actual changes (In general, the pattern of intercorrelations was highly similar for perceived and actual change. In both cases, all of the intercorrelations were positive, except that change in Neuroticism was negatively correlated with change in each of the other four dimensions. The few discrepancies involved differences in magnitude rather than direction. For example, actual change in Conscientiousness correlated .25 with actual change in Extraversion, whereas perceived changes in these two variables did not correlate significantly (r = .10; ns). 

Replication:
We will replicate the exact analyses outlined and numbered above. There are a couple instances where the exact type of analyses is unclear. Specifically, for (3 and 5), it is unclear whether the authors conducted a t-test or ANOVA with contrasts; for (12), it is unclear which operationalization of perceived change grouping the authors used (three vs five groups). For these, we will use a t-test and both the group operationalizations, respectively. Results from the present study will be evaluated against those reported in the two target studies; conclusions will be based on the relative similarity of significance, direction, and magnitude of effect sizes reported across the studies.

Extension:
	In addition to the replications, we hope to extend this work by evaluating additional research questions and using more robust statistical models. First, we are interested in determining the extent to which young adults think their broad personality or individual Big 5 traits will change and whether this anticipatory change is associated with actual change. We will mirror all analyses note above by replacing perceived change with anticipatory change. Consistent with the “End of History Illusion” (Quoidbach, Gilbert, & Wilson, 2013) and self-enhancement literature, we hypothesize that participants will anticipate positive personality change. 
	Second, we are interested in determining whether optimism is associated with anticipatory personality change and/or actual personality change. Consistent with self-enhancement literature, we hypothesize that participants with greater optimism will anticipate greater positive personality change. 

 

	Third, we will analyze the above research questions (i.e., is perceived change associated with actual change; are optimism and anticipatory change associated with actual change) using latent growth curve models since we have eight measures of personality whereas both original studies only had two measures of personality, respectively. This procedure will provide a more reliable estimate of personality change. We will conduct these analyses in a structural equation modeling framework using the R package “lavaan.” We will test for measurement invariance using criteria recommended by Little (2013): change in CFI by .01; if scale invariance is not satisfied due to problems with 25% or fewer items, we will identify the one or two items to drop to achieve scale invariance; if there are more than two item, we attempt second order growth models or abandon this test. Else, models will first be run with freely estimated parameters such that the path estimate for the personality change slope at time one will be fixed to zero, time eight will be fixed to one, and paths in-between will be free to vary. Subsequent models will add constraints to test for linear and non-linear effects. We will set time zero to the midpoint of the study if we encounter strong correlations between the latent intercepts and slopes. If results do not change across models, conclusions will be made from the most parsimonious model; if results do change, a chi-square difference statistic will determine which model to base conclusions from. 

Known differences from original studies: Herbst and colleagues (2000) used the NEO-PI-R whereas we will be using the BFI; however, these two measures have factor convergences ranging from .71 to .84 without correcting for attenuation (Reynolds & Clark, 2001). The study duration (theirs: 6 to 9 years versus ours: 4 years) and sample descriptives (theirs: middle-aged college alumni versus ours: current college students) will differ between studies. 

Robins and colleagues (2005) used the 60-item NEO-FFI whereas we will be using the BFI; however, these two measures have mean factor convergence of .73 without correcting for attenuation (John & Srivastava, 1999). When the study took place (theirs: 1990s vs ours: 2010s) and sample descriptives (students from theirs: UC-B vs ours: UT-D).

Both of these studies used a subset of data from a parent study, both of which differed in the sort of variables collected from our parent study.

Name or brief description of dataset: The present study uses a subset of data collected from the “College Life Study.” The parent study was designed as a longitudinal study of college student adjustment and development.

Is this data open or publicly available? The variables used in these analyses will be posted when the paper is submitted.

How can the data be accessed? Robert Ackerman and Courtney Brecheen collected these data.

Date of download or access: Andrew Rakhshani and Richard Lucas will access these data after submission of this registration.

Is a codebook available? Packets of questionnaires and data keys are available upon request.

Study Title: Do Expectations and Perceptions of Personality Trait Change in College Students Match Reality?  

Authors: Andrew Rakhshani, Brent Donnellan, Richard Lucas, Courtney Brecheen, & Robert Ackerman

Description: 
	This study aims to conceptually replicate two studies (Herbst, McCrae, Costa, Feaganes, & Siegler, 2000; Robins, Noftle, Trzesniewski, & Roberts, 2005) that compared perceived versus actual personality change and extend these works by also evaluating anticipatory personality change. We will conduct secondary analyses on a large, longitudinal dataset of a student cohort followed across four years of college. We intend to emulate the analyses described in each of the target studies and conduct additional analyses relating to anticipated personality change.
	Herbst and colleagues (2000) sought to determine whether self-reported perceived change in personality was associated with actual changes based on 6 to 9-year follow-up data of middle-aged adults. Participants completed the 240-item NEO-PI-R at baseline and again at follow-up. At follow-up participants were also asked to report on how they had changed since their intake using two measures of change. The first was a single item measure reflecting three perceived change groups (i.e., changed a good deal, changed little, or stayed pretty much the same). The second asked whether participants increased, decreased, or stayed the same on each of the Big 5 dimensions (e.g., Extraversion: “compared to how you were six years ago, how lively, cheerful, and sociable are you now?”). Analyses and results were presented as follows: 
(1) frequencies of perceived change groups (52% stayed the same, 39% changed a little, 9% changed a good deal); 
(2) chi-square test of perceived change groups by gender (men: 54% stayed the same, 38% changed a little, 8% changed a good deal; women: 48% stayed the same, 41% changed a little, 11% changed a good deal; slightly more women reported change 2(2, N = 2,241) = 7.7, p = .02);
(3) compared stability coefficients across perceived change groups by Big 5 factor (see table below); 
 
(4) compared profile stability coefficients across perceived change groups (see table above); 
(5) compared baseline and post (respectively) factor and facet (cannot replicate) scores across perceived change groups (specific effect sizes were not reported; Respondents who felt they had changed a good deal scored significantly higher in Neuroticism and Openness and lower on Agreeableness than the other two groups on both administrations); 
(6) frequencies of perceived factor-level change (see note in table below); 
 
(7) compared mean level change from baseline to follow-up by direction of perceived change (the factor level perceived change measure) using repeated measures ANOVAs with Scheffe post hoc tests (these effect sizes were reported as partial eta squared for Time by perceived change group interaction; see table above); 
(8) correlation of perceived change by domain and residual gain score (“the raw change score corrected for initial level”) for the same domain (All five correlations were positive and significant, ranging in magnitude of .10 for Agreeableness to .24 for Neuroticism; On average, perceptions of change accounted for less than 3% of the variance in measured change); and 
(9) percentage of discordance of perceived change group and actual change (Same group had significant declines in all but Agreeableness; More group increased only in Neuroticism and Agreeableness; Less group showed significant declines in all but A; 80% of the comparisons are discordant for the self-perceived Same group, 60% for the More group, 20% for the Less group).
	
Robins and colleagues (2005) sought to determine (1) the extent and in what ways young adults think their personality changes and (2) how much perceived change was associated with actual change. Their study included a third purpose involving a host of additional measures that our dataset does not include so everything to follow will reflect the two parts we can replicate. They followed a group of 295 young adults for six waves across four years of college. Participants completed the 60-item NEO-FFI during the first week of college and again at the end of the fourth year. At the end of the fourth year, participants were also asked to indicate how they had changed (1 = decreased to 5 = increased) since entering college using a single item for each Big 5 factor. To assess actual personality change, they regressed each year four factor score on the corresponding week one factor score and saved the standardized residuals. Relevant analyses were presented as follows: 
(10) frequencies of perceived change grouped by decreased, stayed the same, and increased for each Big 5 factor (Almost everyone (98%) believed that they had changed on at least one factor; see table below); 
(11) actual mean-level personality change reported as Cohen’s d (see table below); 

 
(12) correlations between perceived and actual change by Big 5 factor (see table below); and 
 
(13) footnote noting comparisons of the intercorrelations among perceived changes and the intercorrelations among actual changes (In general, the pattern of intercorrelations was highly similar for perceived and actual change. In both cases, all of the intercorrelations were positive, except that change in Neuroticism was negatively correlated with change in each of the other four dimensions. The few discrepancies involved differences in magnitude rather than direction. For example, actual change in Conscientiousness correlated .25 with actual change in Extraversion, whereas perceived changes in these two variables did not correlate significantly (r = .10; ns). 

Replication:
We will replicate the exact analyses outlined and numbered above. There are a couple instances where the exact type of analyses is unclear. Specifically, for (3 and 5), it is unclear whether the authors conducted a t-test or ANOVA with contrasts; for (12), it is unclear which operationalization of perceived change grouping the authors used (three vs five groups). For these, we will use a t-test and both the group operationalizations, respectively. Results from the present study will be evaluated against those reported in the two target studies; conclusions will be based on the relative similarity of significance, direction, and magnitude of effect sizes reported across the studies.

Extension:
	In addition to the replications, we hope to extend this work by evaluating additional research questions and using more robust statistical models. First, we are interested in determining the extent to which young adults think their broad personality or individual Big 5 traits will change and whether this anticipatory change is associated with actual change. We will mirror all analyses note above by replacing perceived change with anticipatory change. Consistent with the “End of History Illusion” (Quoidbach, Gilbert, & Wilson, 2013) and self-enhancement literature, we hypothesize that participants will anticipate positive personality change. 
	Second, we are interested in determining whether optimism is associated with anticipatory personality change and/or actual personality change. Consistent with self-enhancement literature, we hypothesize that participants with greater optimism will anticipate greater positive personality change. 

 

	Third, we will analyze the above research questions (i.e., is perceived change associated with actual change; are optimism and anticipatory change associated with actual change) using latent growth curve models since we have eight measures of personality whereas both original studies only had two measures of personality, respectively. This procedure will provide a more reliable estimate of personality change. We will conduct these analyses in a structural equation modeling framework using the R package “lavaan.” We will test for measurement invariance using criteria recommended by Little (2013): change in CFI by .01; if scale invariance is not satisfied due to problems with 25% or fewer items, we will identify the one or two items to drop to achieve scale invariance; if there are more than two item, we attempt second order growth models or abandon this test. Else, models will first be run with freely estimated parameters such that the path estimate for the personality change slope at time one will be fixed to zero, time eight will be fixed to one, and paths in-between will be free to vary. Subsequent models will add constraints to test for linear and non-linear effects. We will set time zero to the midpoint of the study if we encounter strong correlations between the latent intercepts and slopes. If results do not change across models, conclusions will be made from the most parsimonious model; if results do change, a chi-square difference statistic will determine which model to base conclusions from.

Robins and colleagues (2005) used the 60-item NEO-FFI whereas we will be using the BFI; however, these two measures have mean factor convergence of .73 without correcting for attenuation (John & Srivastava, 1999). When the study took place (theirs: 1990s vs ours: 2010s) and sample descriptives (students from theirs: UC-B vs ours: UT-D).

Both of these studies used a subset of data from a parent study, both of which differed in the sort of variables collected from our parent study.

title_r: Foodie Calls - A Preregistered Replication Study
abstract_r: When it comes to the question of who is going to pay on a first date, it is not always clear how the bill is shared. While the consensus is hard to reach in many societies, gender roles, which are greatly impacted by culture, play a huge role in determining the answer to this highly debated question. In societies where traditional gender roles and norms are clearly defined and exercised, it might be expected that it is usually men who pay the bill on a first date (Delucia, 1987; Jaramillo-Sierra &amp; Allen, 2013; Wu et al., 2021). In a study based on a US sample, Collisson and colleagues (2020) reported that some women, especially the ones with dark personality traits and traditional gender role beliefs are prone to abuse men in order to receive a free meal on a first date without feeling any actual romantic attraction. However, the impact of Dark Triad personality traits might be irrelevant in circumstances, if traditional gender roles are more explicitly pronounced in society because of the expected norms that suggest men should always pay. The aim of this study is to test the impact of the Dark Triad personality traits on the “foodie call” behavior, which refers to the situation “where a person, despite a lack of romantic attraction to a suitor, chooses to go on a date to get a free meal” (Collisson et al., 2020, p. 425). The study is designed as a pre-registered replication study. The materials are presented on the OSF website.

title_r: Are STEM Faculty Biased Against Female Applicants? A Robust Replication and Extension of Moss-Racusin and Colleagues (2012)
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

Abstract (as of 6/1/20): 

In a seminal study investigating gender bias in academic science, Moss-Racusin et al. (2012) found bias against female lab manager applicants with respect to competence, hireability, mentoring, and salary conferral. This topic will be revisited through four studies--two direct replications, one extension, and a meta analysis. The present set of studies, all using the same methods and materials as the original, will sample from a larger and broader pool of faculty, collectively representing the breadth of STEM disciplines at R1 universities across the United States. The proposed studies will have high power to detect smaller effect sizes than in the original. Furthermore, a priori criteria have been explicitly articulated for what will be accepted as hypothesis confirmation and replication, and for evidence of gender bias. The pre-registered data analysis plans will provide a strong test assessing the replicability of Moss-Racusin et al. (2012)’s finding that STEM faculty were biased against women who applied for a lab manager position.

title_r: The Effect of Thinking About Being Excluded by God on Well-Being: A Replication and Extension
abstract_r: Prior research has provided initial evidence that thinking about being excluded by God lowers self-reported well-being in a Dutch sample of Christian students. The current research sought to replicate this finding in two studies. The first experiment recruited a USA sample of Christian students from a secular and religious school. The second experiment recruited a USA online sample of Christians contacted via Mechanical Turk. Results of these two studies replicated the initial finding that thinking about being excluded by God lowers self-reported well-being relative to thinking about being included by God, or contemplating that God created the earth. Moreover, a mini-meta analysis of the original study and the current two studies added the novel insight that thinking about being included by God increased well-being relative to contemplating that God created the earth. Overall, these results show how people’s perceived relationship with God may influence their quality of life.

title_r: The relationship between anhedonia and delay discounting task: a replication of Lempert and Pizzagalli (2010) study
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

summary: The purpose of this study was to replicate that of Lempert and Pizzagalli (2010), which examined the relationship between anhedonia and the delay discounting task (DDT). Patients with major depressive disorder (MDD) exhibit various symptoms such as depressive mood, anhedonia, and insomnia. Anhedonia is a key symptom of MDD and refers to a loss of positive feeling and a decrease in responsiveness to reward. The DDT has often been used to research MDD and reward responsivity. In DDT, a comparison is made between participants who choose to receive small rewards immediately and those who opt for larger rewards after a delay. Patients with MDD prefer an immediate reward because of their pessimism about the future and their impulsivity. However, in the case of high anhedonia, patients are assumed to prefer the larger rewards after a delay because of their decreased responsiveness to reward. Lempert and Pizzagalli (2010) examine how anhedonia affects DDT; they found a significant negative correlation (r = -0.42) between anhedonia and discounting rate. Thus, anhedonic participants appeared to prefer a larger reward after a longer delay. Lempert and Pizzagalli (2010) argued that anhedonic people have low impulsivity for immediate rewards. This finding is important in clarifying the decision mechanism in depression. However, in many fields of psychological study, there exists a question of reproductivity. The findings of Lempert and Pizzagalli (2010) also did not agree with those of other studies related to anhedonia and delay discounting rate (Cai et al., 2018; Pulcu et al., 2014). Therefore, we will conduct a replication study of Lempert and Pizzagalli’s (2010) study. We will conduct our study using the same setting and analysis as those of Lempert and Pizzagalli (2010)and examine the relationship between anhedonia and delay discounting rate.

title_r: Replication and extension of: Large language models associate Muslims with violence by Abid et al., 2021
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

The main purpose of this study is to replicate and extend the results in Abid et al. (2021; Nature Machine Intelligence). Building on preliminary evidence provided by the creators of GPT-2 and GPT-3 (state-of-the-art text generation algorithms; Radford et al., 2019; Brown et al., 2020), the authors showed biased automated text generation when religious identities are cued in text completion prompts. GPT-3 completions for prompts formatted as “Two X walk into a” contained violent content much more often if X was replaced with “Muslims” rather than adjectives signifying other major religions. Since the smallest difference was found between “Muslim” and “Christian”, our replication attempt focuses on this more conservative measure of the model’s religion bias. However, we include the “Hindu” category as well to control for the impact of majority/minority difference between “Muslim” and “Christian”.
We extend these results by exploring whether naming specific individuals reduces the propensity of the model to rely on biased group-level representations. For instance, using “Y walks into a” where Y is replaced with a common Muslim name compared with names common among adherents of Christianity and Hinduism. 
We also examine whether the model is sensitive to differing degrees of genericity in the main referent of prompts, which can vary along a continuum. Generic kinds like “Muslim” lie near one end of the spectrum. Individual celebrities whose personal information presumably features strongly in GPT-3’s training data (from CommonCrawl.org), lie near the other end. Common names associated with social kinds like “Muslim” (e.g., Ali Islam) are somewhere in-between, albeit closer to the specific end of the genericity spectrum. We expect reduced bias as the specificity of the prompts are increased.

summary: The attached Word document contains structured, detailed descriptions of procedures for a replication of Abid et al.'s (2021) results, with particular attention paid to minor adjustments made by the current authors. It also contains theoretical and practical justifications for the extension based on the linguistic notion of genericity, as well as detailed information about the procedures and materials for that extension. Potential follow-up experiments are also mentioned.

title_r: Tackett lab hormones replication project
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

summary: The present study is an attempt to reproduce, in an independent pre-adolescent sample, analyses from three studies examining the interaction between personality traits and hormones in predicting youth externalizing behavior.  The three papers are as follows: 

A. Reardon, K. W., Herzhoff, K., & Tackett, J. L. (2015). Adolescent personality as risk and resiliency in the testosterone-externalizing association. Journal of Research on Adolescence, 26, 390-402.

B. Tackett, J. L., Herzhoff, K., Harden, K. P., Page-Gould, E., & Josephs, R. A. (2014). Personality x hormone interactions in adolescent externalizing psychopathology. Personality Disorders: Theory, Research, and Treatment. 5, 235-246. 

C. Tackett, J. L., Reardon, K. W., Herzhoff, K., Page-Gould, E., Harden, K. P., & Josephs, R. A. (2015). Estradiol and cortisol interactions in youth externalizing psychopathology. Psychoneuroendocrinology, 55, 146-153. 

Sample: This replication effort will be conducted in an already-collected sample of 350 youth between the ages of 8 and 11. 

Variables: We will use variables indexing hormones, personality traits, and externalizing behavior. 

1. youth hormone levels as measured via a baseline sample of saliva collected 30 minutes after arrival to the lab. The samples were collected using a passive drool method, frozen, and immunoassayed in an independent lab. We will use the measurements of cortisol, testosterone, and estradiol (E2). 

2. parent-reported youth personality pathology traits as measured by the Dimensional Personality Symptom Itempool (DIPSI; De Clercq, De Fruyt, Van Leeuwen, & Mervielde, 2006). We will focus specifically on the higher-order trait dimension of Disagreeableness. 

3. parent-reported youth behavior as measured by the Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL; Achenbach & Rescorla, 2001). We will focus specifically on the broadband Externalizing Problems scale. 

Hypotheses: We are aiming to replicate the findings from each of these three previous studies in a larger sample. This sample diverges from the original sample not only in size, but also in age (pre-adolescent versus adolescent) and in much greater racial/ethnic and socioeconomic diversity.

A. Reardon et al., 2015: This study demonstrated that testosterone was associated with externalizing behavior, but only for youth with low levels of self-regulatory personality. Thus, we hypothesize that testosterone will be predictive of externalizing behavior, but only for those youth high on disagreeableness. We hypothesize that there will be no relationship between testosterone and externalizing behavior for those youth low in disagreeableness. 

B. Tackett et al., 2014: This study found that testosterone was associated with externalizing behavior, but only when cortisol was low, and only among youth high on trait disagreeableness. Thus, we hypothesize that testosterone will be associated with higher externalizing behavior for those youth who have low cortisol and high levels of disagreeableness, and that there will be no relationship between testosterone and externalizing behavior for those youth low in disagreeableness or high in cortisol. 

C. Tackett et al., 2015: This study found that estradiol was associated with externalizing behavior, but only when cortisol was low and only among youth high on trait disagreeableness. Thus, we hypothesize that estradiol will be associated with higher externalizing behavior for those youth who have low cortisol and high levels of disagreeableness, and that there will be no relationship between estradiol and externalizing behavior for those youth low in disagreeableness or high in cortisol. 

Planned analyses: 

1. For the hormone variables (C, T, and E2), any extreme values will be winsorized. An extreme value will be defined as a value more than 3 standard deviations away from the mean, and this value will be replaced with the next highest observed value in the sample. 

2. We anticipate large skew values, as is typical for hormone variables, and thus all hormone variables will be log-transformed to reduce this skew. 

3. Because we anticipate that boys will have significantly higher T levels than girls, and that girls will have significantly higher E2 levels than boys, these two hormones will be standardized (z-scored) within gender, as is consistent with previous research on gonadal hormones (e.g., Mehta & Josephs, 2010). 

4. Age, gender, and time of waking will be used as covariates in all analyses, so these variables will be standardized. In addition, the predictor variable DIPSI Disagreeableness will be standardized. 

5. We will next create interaction terms: 
    a. T x Disagreeableness
    b. C x Disagreeableness
    c. E2 x Disagreeableness
    d. T x C
    e. E2 x C 
    f. T x C x Disagreeableness
    g. E2 x C x Disagreeableness

6. We will run regression analyses to test the central hypotheses of the three studies: 

A. Reardon et al., 2015: Full regressions testing the interaction between testosterone and disagreeableness will include age, sex, and time of waking as covariates in step 1, main effects for T and Disagreeableness in step 2, and the interaction term between T and Disagreeableness in step 3. 

B. Tackett et al., 2014: Full regressions testing the three way interaction between testosterone, cortisol, and disagreeableness will include age, sex, and time of waking as covariates in step 1, main effects for T, C, and Disagreeableness in step 2, the two-way interaction terms between T, C, and Disagreeableness in step 3, and finally the three-way interaction term between T, C, and Disagreeableness in step 4. 

C. Tackett et al., 2015: Full regressions testing the three way interaction between estradiol, cortisol, and disagreeableness will include age, sex, and time of waking as covariates in step 1, main effects for E2, C, and Disagreeableness in step 2, the two-way interaction terms between E2, C, and Disagreeableness in step 3, and finally the three-way interaction term between E2, C, and Disagreeableness in step 4. 

7. Additional analyses to examine potential moderators and specificity of the effects (some of which were directly examined in the previous publications) will include: 

    a. running the regressions using the parent-reported CBCL Internalizing Problems scale as an additional covariate, to test specificity of externalizing problems above-and-beyond general psychopathology. We hypothesize that associations will be smaller, but will still show unique associations with externalizing problems.
    b. running the regressions using the Pubertal Development Scale score (PDS) as a covariate instead of age, as hormone levels are affected by physical maturation. Age and pubertal status are highly correlated, so the pattern of results should largely be the same. Nonetheless, there is so little empirical data with these variables in child and adolescent samples that it is important to see how age and pubertal status covariates may differentially impact evidence for these associations, particularly across different stages of puberty. The current study offers substantial power to test this question in a early/pre-pubertal sample.
    c. running the regressions using the time of testing as a covariate, as hormone concentrations vary throughout the day. The pattern of results is anticipated to remain largely similar with this additional covariate. It will be examined because it is sometimes used as a covariate in similar research using a single baseline sample.
    d. running the regressions separately in boys and girls, a practice which is quite common in human psychoneuroendocrinological research, to examine whether the final pattern of results is similar for both boys and girls. We do not have strong a priori hypotheses for gender differences in these relationships, and the previous publications did not find meaningful evidence for gender differences. 
    e. running the regressions replacing the DIPSI Disagreeableness higher-order scale with the 12 lower-order facets of Disagreeableness. Facet-level analyses offer a more fine-grained examination of those aspects of self-regulatory personality that are involved in these associations (analyses are consistent with Tackett et al., 2014).
    f. examining race/ethnicity as a potential moderator. Evidence indicates different hormone levels across race/ethnic groups, but studies rarely have adequate racial and ethnic diversity to directly examine hormone-behavior associations between groups. Given the lack of previous studies on this specific research question, such analyses would be descriptive.

title_r: Does Speed of Recognition predict Two-Alternatives Forced-Choice Performance? Replicating and Extending Starns, Dubé, and Frelinger (2018)
abstract_r: Does the speed of single-word recognition errors predict performance in subsequent two-alternative forced-choice (2AFC) trials that include the error item? Starns, Dubé, and Frelinger (2018) found effects of this kind in two experiments and account for them in terms of a continuous memory-strength signal guiding recognition decisions. In the 2AFC task, Starns et al. (2018) always paired an item that had been responded to falsely in a preceding single-word recognition task with an item that had been responded to correctly. Participants were instructed to identify and correct the error made in the single-word recognition test via their response in the 2AFC trial. As suggested by Malejka and Bröder (2016) for a source memory task, feedback regarding error items can indeed influence memory decisions. The present study is an adversarial collaboration that aims (a) to replicate Starns et al.’s (2018) results in a replication condition and (b) to test whether the effects of error speed reflect an artefact due to an error-correction strategy that uses response latency as a heuristic cue. For this purpose, we will implement a replication as well as an extension condition in which error feedback is removed. This study will contribute to the broader research question of whether a continuous memory-strength signal or discrete states underlie recognition decisions.

title_r: The Possible Unemployment Cost of Average Inflation Below a Credible Target. A Replication Study of Svensson (American Economic Journal: Macroeconomics, 2015)
abstract_r: This paper replicates the main analysis of Svensson (2015) with some expansion to the original analysis, mainly for the United States. Overall, the replication exercise successfully confirms the conclusions of Svensson (2015). In both Sweden and the United States, empirical evidence sup- ports the existence of a non-vertical long run Phillips curve. The slope of the long run Phillips curve recorded -0.75 in Sweden and -0.23 in the United States. While the average inflation rate in the United States was very close to its targeted level, the average inflation rate in Sweden was 0.6 per- centage points below its targeted level over the sample period. The deviation of inflation rate from its targeted level in Sweden resulted in an unemployment cost equivalent to 0.8 percentage points over the sample period where the average unemployment rate recorded 7.4 percent compared with an estimated 6.6 percent had the average inflation rate been at its targeted level.

title_r: The positive-negative mode link between brain connectivity, demographics, and behavior: A pre-registered replication of Smith et al. 2015
abstract_r: In mental health research, it has proven difficult to find measures of brain function that provide reliable indicators of mental health and well-being, including susceptibility to mental health disorders. Recently, a family of data-driven analyses have provided such reliable measures when applied to large, population-level datasets. In the current pre-registered replication study, we show that the canonical correlation analysis (CCA) methods previously developed using resting-state MRI functional connectivity and subject measures of cognition and behavior from healthy adults are also effective in measuring well-being (a "positive-negative axis") in an independent developmental dataset. Our replication was successful in two out of three of our pre-registered criteria, such that a primary CCA mode's weights displayed a significant positive relationship and explained a significant amount of variance in both functional connectivity and subject measures. The only criteria that was not successful was that compared to other modes the magnitude of variance explained by the primary CCA mode was smaller than predicted, a result which could indicate a developmental trajectory of a primary mode. This replication establishes a signature neurotypical relationship between connectivity and phenotype, opening new avenues of research in neuroscience with clear clinical applications.

title_r: Reproduction Package for FSE 2024 Submission `A Replication Study of Interpolation-Based Hardware Model Checking for Software Verification'
abstract_r:
Reproduction Package A Replication Study of Interpolation-Based Hardware Model Checking for Software Verification Abstract This artifact is a reproduction package for the manuscript “A Replication Study of Interpolation-Based Hardware Model Checking for Software Verification”, submitted to FSE 2024. In the replication study, the transferability of the results reported by two prior publications on interpolation-based hardware model checking to software verification is investigated. The two publications are (1) Interpolation-Sequence-Based Model Checking (Vizel and Grumberg, 2009) and (2) Intertwined Forward-Backward Reachability Analysis Using Interpolants (Vizel, Grumberg, and Shoham, 2013). The purpose of this artifact is to reproduce the experiments conducted to validate the claims made in the above two publications. The artifact consists of source code, precompiled executables, and input data used in the evaluation of the replication study, as well as the results produced from the experiments. Specifically, it includes the source code and binaries of CPAchecker (at revision 44757 of branch “cfa-single-loop-transformation”), which implements the verification algorithms compared in the submitted manuscript, the SV-COMP ’23 benchmark suite, the experimental data generated from the evaluation, and instructions to run the tools and experiments. This reproduction package works best with the SoSy-Lab Virtual Machine, which runs Ubuntu 22.04 LTS. The VM has all the required dependencies installed. If you test this artifact with it, all installation steps below can be skipped. Contents This artifact contains the following items: README.*: this documentation fse2024-paper483.pdf: the manuscript submitted to FSE 2024 License.txt: license information of the artifact cpachecker/: a directory containing the source code and precompiled binaries of CPAchecker sv-benchmarks/: a directory containing the SV-COMP ’23 benchmark tasks used in our evaluation data-submission/: a directory containing the raw and processed data produced from our full evaluation (used in the manuscript, under paper-results/) and from a demo experiment (prepared for this reproduction package, under demo-results/) bench-defs/: a directory containing the benchmark and table definitions of the experiments (used by BenchExec, a framework for reliable benchmarking) This readme file will guide you through the following steps: Execute CPAchecker Perform experiments View the experimental results Execute CPAchecker System requirements for CPAchecker To execute CPAchecker, Java Runtime Environment (JRE) version ≥ 17 is required. For more information, please refer to cpachecker/INSTALL.md. Run verification algorithms in CPAchecker In the replication study, we compared the performance of three interpolation-based verification algorithms, namely IMC (McMillan, 2003), ISMC (Vizel and Grumberg, 2009), and DAR (Vizel, Grumberg, and Shoham, 2013). ISMC and DAR are the algorithms proposed by the two prior publications, respectively, and IMC is the first interpolation-based model-checking approach, which was used as the baseline in the two publications. All the algorithms have been implemented in CPAchecker. Below we list the commands to run the evaluated verification algorithms. These example commands use sv-benchmarks/c/loop-invariants/even.c as the input program. You can replace it with another program. IMC: 
# expected verification result: TRUE cpachecker/scripts/cpa.sh -32 -spec sv-comp-reachability \ -bmc-interpolation \ -setprop cpa.predicate.memoryAllocationsAlwaysSucceed=true \ -setprop cpa.predicate.refinement.verifyInterpolants=true \ -setprop cfa.transformIntoSingleLoop=true \ -setprop imc.fallBack=false \ -setprop imc.loopBoundIncrementStrategyForBMC=CONST \ sv-benchmarks/c/loop-invariants/even.c
ISMC: 
# expected verification result: TRUE cpachecker/scripts/cpa.sh -32 -spec sv-comp-reachability \ -bmc-interpolationSequence \ -setprop cpa.predicate.memoryAllocationsAlwaysSucceed=true \ -setprop cpa.predicate.refinement.verifyInterpolants=true \ -setprop cfa.transformIntoSingleLoop=true \ -setprop imc.fallBack=false \ sv-benchmarks/c/loop-invariants/even.c
DAR: 
# expected verification result: TRUE cpachecker/scripts/cpa.sh -32 -spec sv-comp-reachability \ -bmc-interpolationDualSequence \ -setprop cpa.predicate.memoryAllocationsAlwaysSucceed=true \ -setprop cpa.predicate.refinement.verifyInterpolants=true \ -setprop cfa.transformIntoSingleLoop=true \ -setprop dar.fallBack=false \ sv-benchmarks/c/loop-invariants/even.c
For more information on how to run CPAchecker, see cpachcker/README.md. Understand the output of CPAchecker The following is an example output shown on the console after an analysis is finished. 
[...redacted...] Verification result: TRUE. No property violation found by chosen configuration. More details about the verification run can be found in the directory "./output". Graphical representation included in the file "./output/Report.html".
There are 3 possible outcomes of the verification result: TRUE: the program is “safe”, i.e., it satisfies the given safety property FALSE: the program is “unsafe”, i.e., it contains a violation to the given safety property UNKNOWN: the analysis was inconclusive CPAchecker also generates an HTML report for conveniently browsing the results. Please refer to cpachecker/doc/Report.md for more information. Perform Experiments Install BenchExec We use BenchExec, a framework for reliable benchmarking and resource measurements, to perform our evaluation. Please follow the installation guide to set up the benchmarking environment. Experimental settings The settings are described in the XML file bench-defs/cpachecker-slt.xml. This XML file is used by BenchExec for limiting computing resources and scheduling runs. For the execution of a task, a resource limit of 2 CPU cores, 1800 seconds of CPU time, and 15 GB of memory is imposed. Run the Full Evaluation To run the full experiment over the 8813 benchmark tasks reported in the manuscript, execute the following command. 
benchexec bench-defs/cpachecker-slt.xml \ --tool-directory cpachecker/ -o results/ \ --read-only-dir / --overlay-dir . --hidden-dir /home/
Run Partial Evaluation The full evaluation requires roughly 6 months of CPA time on a 3.40 GHz core. To run the experiment on a subset of benchmark tasks, you could add -t <tasks_name> to the above command, where <task_name> refer to the task names defined in bench-defs/cpachecker-slt.xml. For example: 
benchexec bench-defs/cpachecker-slt.xml \ --tool-directory cpachecker/ -o results/ \ --read-only-dir / --overlay-dir . --hidden-dir /home/ \ -t ReachSafety-BitVectors
If you want to adjust the imposed resource limit, the following options can be used: 
-T <cputime_limit> -M <mem_limit>
For more information about these flags, please refer to benchexec -h. View the Experimental Results Generate Tables After the execution of an experiment, you can generate an interactive HTML by table-generator. Simply run: 
table-generator -x bench-defs/overall-slt-stats.xml \ -f html --no-diff -o results
Note that if the experiment is only performed on a single task set (via -t <tasks_name>), you have to replace bench-defs/overall-slt-stats.xml by bench-defs/subset-slt-stats.xml. Results from Our Experiments The results (both raw and processed data) of the partial run (on ReachSafety-BitVectors) and the full run obtained by our machines are in folders data-submission/demo-results/ and data-submission/paper-results/, respectively. The generated HTML tables are named overall-slt-stats.table.html under each respective folder. In the replication study, there are eight hypotheses extracted from the two prior publications. We list them below to make this document more standalone. For details, please refer to the bundled manuscript. Claims in the ISMC Publication H1.A: ISMC is faster than IMC on tasks with property violation. H1.B: ISMC is faster than IMC when IMC finds a proof only at high unrolling bounds. H1.C: Overall, ISMC is faster than IMC (by 30 % in this experiment). In our experiments, we confirmed H1.A also for software verification, but H1.B and H1.C did not hold. Claims in the DAR Publication H2.A: For DAR, the ratio between iterations using global strengthening to the total number of iterations is less than 0.5 in most tasks. H2.B: IMC finds a proof slower than DAR in many tasks even though it has a smaller convergence length. H2.C: DAR computes more interpolants than IMC. H2.D: DAR’s run-time is more sensitive to the sizes of interpolants than IMC. H2.E: Overall, DAR is faster than IMC (by 36 % in this experiment). In our experiments, we confirmed H2.A and H2.C also for software verification, but H2.B, H2.D, and H2.E did not hold. Here we provide pre-configured links to easily view the corresponding tables/figures shown in the manuscript. title_r: The mediating role of LMX between abusive supervision and work behaviors: A replication and extension
abstract_r: Purpose - – In a replication of a multi-source study by Xu Design/methodology/approach - – The authors collected multi-source data in order to minimize common method bias. The authors conducted regression analyses, Sobel tests, and bootstrapping techniques. Findings - – The authors found support that LMX mediates the negative relationship between abusive supervision and OCBO and OCBI. However, the authors could not replicate the mediating role of LMX in the association between abusive supervision and employees' performance. Similar results were obtained when the data were analyzed with the active-aggressive and passive-aggressive abusive supervision subscales. Research limitations/implications - – Due to the cross-sectional nature of the study, this study does not allow the authors to draw causal conclusions regarding the proposed relationships. Originality/value - – The authors replicated Xu

item34: In our replication study, the interaction effect between employee gender and employee crying on perceived typicality was not statistically significant and thus we were unable to reject the null hypothesis. However, the direction of the effect is in the same direction as the original finding.

item37: Firstly, the participant demographics in the replication study was different as compared to the original study. Our current study’s participants had a much smaller sample size in the current study (32 participants in our current study and 169 participants in the original study), and an average age that was almost 10 years younger than that of the original study, with twice the number of people being unemployed at the point of testing as compared to the original study. These differences could have contributed to our inability to replicate the findings of the original study, as the younger age group and differential employment status of participants in the current study could mean that they might have different types of thinking from participants in the original study, thus affecting their ratings of the perceived typicality of the situation.
Secondly, there is no compensation provided to participants, and this could have affected their motivation to pay attention to the items in the study, resulting in inattentiveness in their responses, that might not have been detected by the manipulation check questions. Singer (2002) found that monetary incentives can be used to motivate participation in individuals, and the authors of the original study (Motro & Ellis, 2017) similarly provided participants with monetary compensation should they be included in their data set. 
Thirdly, the fact that employee Pat shown in the video to participants was a White individual, it could have influenced the perceived psychological realism of the participants of our current study, as they are all Asians, and might have difficulty relating to the situation shown as Pat is of a different ethnicity.  Additionally, in this replication study, the participants were not told to imagine that they were the direct supervisor of Pat, the employee in the video, unlike in the original study as the researchers had deduced it was necessary only for the second hypothesis which was not replicated. Both of these factors might have lessened the psychological realism created for the participants in the present replication, which could have contributed to the non-significant finding.

title_r: Replication and Extension of Nozaradan, Peretz, Missal and Mouraux (2011)
abstract_r: Frequency tagging has been used to capture auditory entrainment to beat and meter in music. Specifically, Nozaradan, Peretz, Missal and Mouraux (2011) instructed listeners to imagine either a binary or ternary metrical pattern while listening to an isochronous auditory stimulus and recorded cortical responses using electroencephalography (EEG). The amplitude of brain activity was increased at beat-related frequencies in both imagery conditions. This study inspired other labs to use the frequency tagging approach to examine auditory rhythm perception, and in only 6 years, it has been cited over 250 times on Google Scholar. The frequency tagging technique has been used in several published papers since 2011 and it is being used increasingly in research presented at recent research conferences and symposia. However, this seminal study has not been replicated. This registered report will detail the results of multiple independent conceptual replications of Nozaradan et al. (2011), all of which will follow the same vetted protocol.
